data.title: this Binding
data.subtitle: Call-site rules vs lexical this in arrows

cards.front: Variables vs this — one sentence each?
cards.meaning: Variable lookup is lexical (where code was written). For ordinary functions, this is decided mostly by how the function is called (call site), plus new, bind, and arrows (lexical this). Ordinary this is not a variable on the scope chain.

Highest to lowest: new (the instance), explicit (call/apply/bind), implicit (obj.method()), default (bare fn() → undefined in strict, global in sloppy). Arrows ignore this ladder — use enclosing lexical this.

cards.front: Bare fn() — this in strict vs sloppy?
cards.meaning: Strict (modules, class bodies, 'use strict'): undefined. Sloppy: global object (globalThis). Modern React/TS/ESM → expect undefined on detached calls, not window.
cards.example: 'use strict'; function f() { return this; } f(); // undefined

cards.meaning: Default binding — not obj. Implicit binding needs receiver.method(). Same family: setTimeout(obj.method, 0), const { greet } = obj; greet(). In strict, reading this.x throws. Fix: obj.read.bind(obj), or an arrow that captures lexical this.
cards.notes: strict: TypeError reading property of undefined.

cards.meaning: The object immediately left of the final call — here obj.nested, not obj. Only the last link before () is the receiver.
Without thisArg, this is not user. With thisArg user, explicit thisArg is OK. Wrapping [1].forEach(() => user.print()) keeps the call shape user.print().

call: invoke immediately with listed args. apply: invoke immediately with args as an array (or array-like). bind: return a new function permanently tied to thisArg (and optional partial args); it does not mutate the original. add.bind(null, 10)(5) is 15.

cards.front: call/apply on an already-bound function — new this?
cards.meaning: Not the way beginners expect. Bound functions ignore later implicit/default calls, and call/apply do not re-bind this to a new target — the bound this sticks.

cards.front: call/apply with thisArg null or undefined?
cards.meaning: Strict mode: this is actually that value (null or undefined). Sloppy mode: they coerce to the global object.

cards.front: What does new Fn(...args) roughly do?
cards.meaning: (1) Create a new ordinary object. (2) Set that object’s prototype link from Fn.prototype. (3) Call Fn with this bound to the new object. (4) If the constructor returns an object, that object is the result; otherwise use the new object.
cards.example: function User(name) { this.name = name; } const u = new User('Ada'); u.name; // 'Ada'

cards.front: new Bound() when F was bound to obj?
cards.meaning: new wins over bind’s thisArg for construction — this is the new instance, not obj. new has highest precedence among ordinary call-site rules.
cards.example: const Bound = F.bind(obj); const x = new Bound(); x.tag; // 'instance'

cards.meaning: Default this — pollutes global, or throws in strict when assigning this.name. That is why constructors are capitalized by convention and why classes force new.

cards.front: Do arrow functions get this from the four call-site rules?
cards.meaning: No. They have no own this binding. Evaluating this inside an arrow resolves like a variable in the enclosing lexical scope. They also have no own arguments; new arrow → TypeError; no own super the way methods do.

Not the object. Object literals don’t create a this binding for the arrow; it captures lexical this from outside (often undefined in modules), not implicit obj. Do not use arrows as prototype methods that need per-call receivers.
cards.example: obj.regular(); // this=obj. obj.arrow(); // lexical, typically undefined name.

cards.front: Why arrow in setTimeout inside start() fixes this.ms?
cards.meaning: Arrow has no own this; it uses this from enclosing start() where implicit binding made this the timer object. A regular function callback gets default binding, not the timer.
cards.example:
timer.start(); // arrow logs this.ms from timer
setTimeout(function () { console.log(this.ms); } // default, not timer2

cards.meaning: obj if f was called as obj.f() — the arrow captured this from f’s implicit binding at the call that created it.
cards.example: const obj = { f() { return () => this; } }; const arrow = obj.f(); arrow(); // obj

cards.meaning: TypeError. Arrow functions cannot be used as constructors.

React invokes a bare function reference, not component.handleClick(), so implicit binding never applies; class bodies are strict → this is undefined → this.props throws. Fixes: constructor bind; class field arrow handleClick = () => {} (lexical instance this); inline onClick={() => this.handleClick()}. Function components sidestep this because there is no this.
cards.notes: Modern codebases often avoid the issue with function components.
